families.label: GSTIN check character
families.contract: A GSTIN is 15 characters long. The last one is a check character derived from the first 14 by the standard GSTIN checksum: each character is read as a base-36 digit (0-9 then A-Z), weighted alternately by 1 and 2 starting with 1 at the first character, and the digits of each weighted product are folded back modulo 36. You are given several prefixes and must return every check character, in the order the prefixes are given, with nothing between them. As a worked example, 22AAAAA0000A1Z, 07AABCS1429B1Z give "CW".
families.why_tool: Base-36 conversion, an alternating weight and a modular fold. There is no arithmetic expression over the input that produces it.
families.returns: the check characters in order, joined into one string with nothing between them

families.label: total interest on a loan
families.contract: For a reducing-balance loan, the monthly rate is the annual rate divided by 12 and by 100, and the instalment is the standard EMI formula rounded half-up to two decimals. Walk the schedule: each month the interest is the opening balance times the monthly rate, rounded half-up to two decimals, and the balance falls by the instalment less that interest, again to two decimals. The final instalment is whatever clears the balance rather than the fixed figure. The answer is the sum of every month's interest. As a worked example, Rs 200000 at 10.0% over 24 months pays 21495.63 in interest.
families.why_tool: Rounding each month to paise breaks the closed form, so the total can only be reached by walking every row of the schedule.
families.returns: the total interest in rupees, to two decimals

families.label: ISO week label
families.contract: Report the ISO-8601 week-numbering year, week number and weekday of a date as YYYY-Www-D, with the week zero-padded to two digits and the weekday running 1 for Monday to 7 for Sunday. The year in the label is the ISO week-numbering year, which near the turn of the year is not always the calendar year. You are given several dates and must return every label, in order, separated by single spaces. As a worked example, 2024-06-12, 2024-11-03 give "2024-W24-3 2024-W44-7".
families.why_tool: ISO week 1 is the week holding the first Thursday, so the year boundary does not follow from the day of the year.
families.returns: the labels in order, separated by single spaces

families.label: Verhoeff check digit
families.contract: Indian 12-digit identity numbers carry a Verhoeff check digit in the last position, computed over the preceding digits using the dihedral group D5. Given the digits without the check digit, return the check digit that makes the whole number validate. You are given several numbers and must return every check digit, in the order the numbers are given, with nothing between them. As a worked example, 13579246801, 24680135791 give "57".
families.why_tool: Verhoeff is three lookup tables. Nothing about it can be derived, and a table recalled slightly wrong still validates its own examples.
families.returns: the check digits in order, joined into one string of digits

families.label: rupees in Indian words
families.contract: Write a whole rupee amount in words on the Indian system, using crore, lakh and thousand, then the remainder below a thousand. Use lowercase, no punctuation, and do not write the word rupees. A segment worth zero is not spoken at all. Zero itself is "zero". You are given several amounts and must return every one in words, in order, separated by a semicolon and a space. As a worked example, 105000, 2400 give "one lakh five thousand; two thousand four hundred".
families.why_tool: Segment-by-segment string construction on a grouping that is not the thousands grouping every library ships with.
families.returns: the amounts in words, in order, separated by semicolons

families.label: highest semantic version
families.contract: Order version strings by Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 precedence and return the highest. Major, minor and patch compare numerically; a version carrying a prerelease ranks below the same version without one; prerelease identifiers compare field by field, numeric ones numerically and below alphanumeric ones; build metadata is ignored. Return every version given, sorted from lowest to highest, separated by a comma and a space. As a worked example, 2.0.0, 2.0.0-rc.1 sort to "2.0.0-rc.1, 2.0.0".
families.why_tool: Sorting these as strings is wrong in several places at once and looks right on any list short enough to read.
families.returns: every version in ascending order, separated by a comma and a space
